outcome: No change to the Lindelöf hypothesis itself (the statement that ζ(1/2+it) = o(t^ε) for all ε>0, equivalently μ(1/2)=0) has been found since 26 January 2024. The best unconditional bound on the growth exponent μ(1/2) remains Bourgain's μ(1/2) ≤ 13/84 (2016/2017), unimproved in the window.
summary: The Lindelöf hypothesis, as stated in the frozen bullet, is that ζ(1/2+it) = o(t^ε) for every ε>0, equivalent to the growth exponent μ(1/2) being exactly 0. The best unconditional upper bound on μ(1/2) is still Bourgain's μ(1/2) ≤ 13/84 ≈ 0.1548, from 'Decoupling, exponential sums and the Riemann zeta function' (arXiv:1408.5794, published J. Amer. Math. Soc. 2017) — work that predates the frozen revision by years and shows no post-January-2024 improvement in any source I found (Terence Tao's blog tag page for the Riemann zeta function, the current Wikipedia article, and multiple targeted searches for 'mu(1/2) improvement 2024/2025/2026'). Several pieces of adjacent work appeared in the window, none of which change what a careful reader would write in this bullet: (1) Hiary, Patel & Yang (J. Number Theory 256 (2024), 195–217; the 'HPY 2024' paper the triage flagged) improve the explicit *constant* in the classical convexity-type bound |ζ(1/2+it)| ≤ C·t^{1/6}\log t from 0.77 down to 0.618 — this bound is a much weaker (Weyl/convexity-class, exponent 1/6 not 13/84) statement than the current subconvexity record, and tightening its leading constant says nothing about whether the o(t^ε) growth rate holds; it is a related result, not a case of the stated hypothesis, and uses no AI ('computational calculations' in the abstract refers to numerical/interval verification, not a learned model). (2) Michael Revers's arXiv:2602.05614 (submitted 5 Feb 2026) further tightens that same constant, again on the t^{1/6}\log t bound, again with no AI mentioned and no change to μ(1/2). (3) Guth & Maynard's 'New large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials' (arXiv:2405.20552, 31 May 2024, revised 7 Apr 2026) is a genuine breakthrough — the first improvement to Ingham's 1940 zero-density estimate — but it is a zero-density result (Montgomery's 'Problem B' / the density hypothesis, N(σ,T) bounds), a different, if related, open problem on the same Wikipedia list; it does not bound |ζ(1/2+it)| itself and is explicitly a variant under §3.1, not a restriction of the Lindelöf statement. (4) arXiv:2505.14228, 'The Lindelöf Hypothesis for Zeta Zero Ordinates,' despite its title, studies a Lindelöf-type statement for exponential sums over the ordinates of zeta zeros (in the sense of Gonek et al.) — a differently-posed analogue sharing the name, not the classical hypothesis about ζ(1/2+it) itself; a related problem, not a case. (5) In searching for AI involvement in this area I found Anthropic's August 2026 announcement that an unreleased Claude research model raised the known lower bound on the proportion of non-trivial zeta zeros on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2% (reviewed by Anthropic mathematicians and outside experts Brian Conrey and Dan Goldston, with an accompanying Lean formalization) — this is a zero-density/proportion-on-critical-line result tied to the Riemann Hypothesis, not the Lindelöf hypothesis, and belongs (if anywhere) to a different bullet on the list. No AI system was found to be involved in any work that touches the Lindelöf hypothesis or the μ(1/2) exponent specifically. I therefore classify this as open with no_change_found true and ai_role none.
competing_reading: One could argue the Hiary-Patel-Yang/Revers constant-tightening sequence is 'progress' in a loose sense, since it improves the numerically best-known explicit pointwise bound on |ζ(1/2+it)| in absolute terms. But the relevant Wikipedia bullet concerns the *hypothesis* — whether ζ(1/2+it)=o(t^ε) for every ε — and the bound being tightened is a t^{1/6}\log t (Weyl-class) bound, three orders of magnitude weaker in exponent than the sharpest known subconvexity bound (13/84≈0.1548), which itself is untouched. Tightening a constant on a strictly weaker classical bound changes nothing a careful person would write about the status of the hypothesis or of μ(1/2), so I do not classify it as `progress`. If a future record specifically improves Bourgain's 13/84 exponent (even fractionally), that would be `progress` with `ai_role` to be determined by its authors' own account.
what_would_settle_it: Any peer-reviewed or arXiv result stating a new unconditional upper bound on μ(1/2) strictly below 13/84, or any proof/disproof of ζ(1/2+it)=o(t^ε) for all ε, dated after 26 January 2024.
